newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African shares seen tailing Wall St up next week.
newsitem.headline: S.African shares seen tailing Wall St up next week.

text.p: South African shares are seen receiving a belated Christmas present of sturdy gains next week as they resume tailing Wall Street, which analysts said on Friday showed few signs of cooling its recent rise.

Local investment fund managers who had not yet returned to work after the Christmas holidays were also seen taking up their posts and loading their portfolios with stocks -- a trend that had already started this week.

"We've still got inflows and there is still money that has to go into the market as a carryover from the December period," Malcolm Chapman, general manager of Absa Asset Management, told Reuters on Friday.
Dealers and analysts said that although the South African market has been out of step with the U.S. recently, it appeared to have started tracking Wall Street again.
The U.S. market has steamed ahead this week, with the Dow Jones industrial average adding over 81 points in the first four days and setting three new record highs.

"We seem to be following Wall Street again, it makes a nice change. That market seems to be its own animal, the fund managers in London tell us the amount of money that is pouring in is mind boggling," a dealer said.

All eyes would, however, later be on the release of key U.S. December jobs data at 1330 GMT for signs of inflationary pressures which could signal a possible hike in interest rates and hit the stock market.

"If the payrolls data is too high and average hourly earnings kick up, it could have a negative impact on the market. But I don't think there is too much risk there," said Matt Brenzel, a portfolio manager at Coronation Asset Management.

Analysts were tentatively upbeat about the outlook for South African gold stocks in the week ahead, following a recovery in bullion on Thursday to above the $358 level after it plumbed 3 -1/4 year lows earlier in the week.

"On precious metals I am cautiously optimistic from the point of view that we have seen a strong run down in the dollar gold price and maybe its a little bit overdone, but certainly I don't expect any fireworks," Brenzel said.

He was more confident about base metal stocks, notably aluminium and steel. "I think the precious metals had a bit of a blip up last year, but they have pulled back and it is now the chance of the base metals," he said.

Amid a dearth of earnings results from large corporates and no major economic indicators due, dealers said stocks would closely watch the bond and rand market, where robust gains have been registered this week.

One concern to traders was that South African industrial shares were charging up too quickly and that a period of consolidation was needed. The index has climbed almost 200 points or 2.5 percent so far this week.
"We need a bit of a correction for the market to stabilise, otherwise when it falls it just collapses in a heap as there is nothing underneath," an equity dealer said.

Another worry for the market was the heavy losses which have dogged the Japanese stock market since early December. On Friday the key Nikkei 225 plunged over four percent taking its slide since early last month to around 20 percent.
"Although there's no real connection between us and Tokyo, it affects sentiment," a dealer said.
